story: Forlandet National Park covers the whole of Prins Karls Forland, an 86-kilometre-long, narrow island off the west coast of Spitsbergen, together with the surrounding territorial waters — about 616 square kilometres of land and some 4,031 of sea. The island is almost cut in two by Forlandsletta, a low coastal plain. North of it runs a chain of sharp alpine peaks; the west coast is lined with wide strand flats and raised beaches, while on the east side wild, steep glaciers reach the sea in several places. The rock is folded and metamorphosed Caledonian bedrock, with younger sedimentary layers in the north-east, and rock glaciers creep down the flanks of the mountains.

The park is the core area for the world's northernmost population of harbour seals, and for the world's northernmost breeding common guillemots. Bird cliffs ring the island, and two bird reserves within the protected area — Forlandsøyane and Plankeholmane — hold large breeding colonies of common eiders and geese; Forlandsøyane is a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention. Barnacle geese and black guillemots breed here, walrus haul out at well-known sites, and a small population of Svalbard reindeer grazes the plains.

The Dutch explorer Willem Barentsz saw the island in 1596. The English whaler Jonas Poole named it Black Point Isle in 1610, and by 1612 English whalers were calling it Prince Charles' Foreland after the son of King James; they kept a temporary whaling station at its northern tip, Fair Foreland, now Fuglehuken. Whaling, Norwegian and Russian overwintering trappers and later mineral prospectors have all left remains on its shores.

Forlandet became one of Svalbard's first three national parks, with Sør-Spitsbergen and Nordvest-Spitsbergen, by royal resolution on 1 June 1973, when more than half of the archipelago was protected. It lies on the shipping route along Spitsbergen's west coast, but there is no settlement and little traffic ashore. Since 2025 ships entering the park's waters may carry no more than 200 passengers.
howItWorks: Svalbard is governed by its own environmental law, the Svalbard Environmental Protection Act, and since 1 January 2026 by a new field-safety regulation (FOR-2025-06-06-940). The whole of Forlandet lies outside Svalbard's travel area, the former management area 10. Independent visitors must notify the Governor of Svalbard (Sysselmesteren) at least four weeks before travelling outside the travel area and wait for the Governor's reply before setting out; they must carry insurance or a guarantee covering search and rescue costs and equipment for raising the alarm and two-way communication. Tour and field operators need the Governor's permission, and residents must also notify the Governor before travelling in Forlandet.

Polar bears are protected. It is forbidden to disturb, attract or pursue them, and you may not travel or stay closer than 300 metres to a polar bear — 500 metres from 1 March to 30 June. Anyone outside the settlements, except participants on organised tours, must know how to protect against polar bear attack and carry suitable means of scaring a bear off; the Governor recommends a rifle as the primary protection. Automatically protected cultural remains — everything from before 1946 — carry a 100-metre safety zone in which you may not pitch a tent (except on frozen, snow-covered ground) or light a fire without permission.

The park's own rules forbid off-road vehicles, landing with aircraft, and flying below 300 metres within one nautical mile of land. Drones and other remote-controlled devices are banned in the air, on the ground and on or under water. Organised tourist landings are allowed only on snow-covered, frozen ground from 1 January to 25 May or at designated landing sites, always with a guide. Keep your distance from wildlife and from protected cultural remains, leave no new tracks and no waste, and take nothing — plants and fossils are protected. In the Forlandsøyane and Plankeholmane bird reserves all traffic, on land and at sea out to 300 metres, is forbidden from 15 May to 15 August.

sightNotes.poi-no-forlandet-forlandsoyane: Three small islands off the west coast of Forlandsletta: a bird reserve and Ramsar site, closed to all traffic from 15 May to 15 August.
sightNotes.poi-no-forlandet-poolepynten: A 1.5-km-long point on Forlandsundet, named after the whaler Jonas Poole.
sightNotes.poi-no-forlandet-monacofjellet: At 1,084 metres the northernmost mountain of the Grampianfjella chain in the north of the island.
sightNotes.poi-no-forlandet-richardlaguna: A lagoon about 7 km long on the island's eastern coast.
sightNotes.poi-no-forlandet-fuglehuken: The northern point of the island — the English whalers' Fair Foreland — with cultural remains on its coast.
sightNotes.poi-no-forlandet-plankeholmane: About twenty skerries and islets off the island's southern tip: a bird reserve closed to all traffic from 15 May to 15 August.

entrances: By sea only, with expedition cruise ships and organised boat trips
planYourVisit.reservations: Independent travellers must notify the Governor of Svalbard at least four weeks ahead and wait for a reply; tour operators need the Governor's permission. The park authority recommends visiting with a cruise ship or an organised operator.
permits: Notification to the Governor of Svalbard for travel outside the travel area, with search-and-rescue insurance
Organised tourist landings only on frozen, snow-covered ground from 1 January to 25 May or at designated landing sites, with a guide
Ships in the park's waters may carry no more than 200 passengers
camping: Camping is governed by the Svalbard Environmental Protection Act; never within 100 metres of protected cultural remains, except on frozen, snow-covered ground
lodging: None on the island; Longyearbyen and Ny-Ålesund are the nearest settlements
seasonalClosures: Forlandsøyane and Plankeholmane bird reserves: no traffic on land or at sea within 300 metres from 15 May to 15 August

chronology.text: The English whaler Jonas Poole names it Black Point Isle.
English whalers call it Prince Charles' Foreland and keep a whaling station at its northern tip.
A royal resolution of 1 June creates Forlandet National Park, one of Svalbard's first three.
A new regulation for Svalbard's original national parks and nature reserves takes effect on 1 May.
Tour operators landing at Fuglehuken must follow site-specific guidelines.
Ships in the park are limited to 200 passengers, tourist landings are confined to designated sites and frozen ground, and drones are banned.
Svalbard's new field-safety regulation takes effect on 1 January.

safety: Polar bears can appear anywhere, at any time of year. Keep at least 300 metres away (500 metres from March to June), carry means of scaring a bear, and never travel ashore without someone trained to use a firearm.
Help is far away and the sea is cold. Notify the Governor, carry two-way communications and insurance, and travel with experienced guides.
Glaciers on the east coast calve into the sea; keep boats well back from glacier fronts.
Walrus and seals on haul-outs are easily disturbed — approach slowly, quietly and never closer than the guide allows.
regulations: Notify the Governor of Svalbard at least four weeks before travelling here as an independent visitor, and carry rescue insurance and two-way communications.
Keep 300 metres from polar bears (500 metres from 1 March to 30 June); do not disturb, attract or pursue them.
No drones, no off-road vehicles, no aircraft landings and no flying below 300 metres within a nautical mile of land.
Bird reserves Forlandsøyane and Plankeholmane are closed from 15 May to 15 August, out to 300 metres from land.
Leave cultural remains from before 1946 untouched, with a 100-metre margin; take no plants or fossils and leave no waste.

fees.title: Svalbard environmental fee
fees.detail: Paid by every visitor to Svalbard except residents: collected with the ticket for the flight out of Svalbard, or by the travel organiser. It goes to the Svalbard Environmental Protection Fund.

weather: Svalbard lies roughly midway between mainland Norway and the North Pole, and its seasons are extreme: in summer it is light around the clock, in winter dark around the clock. Ship-borne visits happen in the summer months, when the sea is open; even then fog, wind and cold can close in quickly, and snow can fall at any time.
directions: Svalbard is about 700 km north of mainland Norway; visitors arrive by air in Longyearbyen. Prins Karls Forland lies west of Spitsbergen, across the sound Forlandsundet, on the shipping route along the west coast. There is no settlement and there are no facilities on the island; it is reached only by boat. The park authority advises visiting with a cruise ship or an organised operator, because the parks are hard to reach and can be dangerous to visit on your own.
